blocks.heading: What this section asks you to do
blocks.text: Explain how the demand for workers and the supply of available workers set the wage in an occupation, and trace what happens in one town when an employer expands.

blocks.heading: The wage as the price of work
blocks.text: A wage is the pay a worker receives for a period of work, quoted in N$ an hour or N$ a month. It is determined in the market for that work: employers demand workers to produce goods and services, workers supply their time and skill, and the wage settles where the number of workers sought matches the number offering to work. Because each occupation and each town has its own pool of workers, the balance - and so the wage - differs from job to job and from place to place.

blocks.heading: Shortage bids up, surplus presses down
blocks.text: Where a new mine near Karibib seeks more trained workers than the town holds at the going wage, employers are likely to bid the wage up to attract and keep staff, because each vacancy left unfilled costs them output. Where a firm closes a production line, more workers offer themselves than employers seek, and pay stalls or falls as job-seekers outnumber posts. A rise in demand for a firm's product works the same way: the firm seeks more workers, and the competition among employers for a limited number of trained people pushes the wage up.

blocks.heading: A packing line in Gobabis
blocks.text: Marula Foods in Gobabis packed fruit with 40 workers at N$5 200 a month. A new pulp contract called for 55 packers; the firm raised the wage to N$6 100, and 15 workers arrived from nearby farms within the month. The extra posts number 55 - 40 = 15 workers, and at the new wage the number sought matched the number offering. In the Netherlands the same balance sets the wage for trained flower sorters at the Aalsmeer auctions: in the weeks before holidays each auction house needs its orders packed at once, and the houses bid up the sorting wage for as long as the rush lasts.

blocks.heading: Who holds the stronger hand
blocks.text: The balance of demand and supply is not the whole story: the wage also depends on the relative bargaining power of the two sides. A worker bargaining alone with a large employer has little power, because the employer can usually find another applicant. Where workers bargain together through a trade union (topic 3.4), the employer risks losing a whole workforce at once in a strike, so the union tends to secure a higher wage than workers acting one by one would. Workers whose skills are hard to replace hold power of their own: a firm with one qualified electrician is likely to pay well to keep her. The balance tips the other way in a town where one large employer faces many job-seekers. A meat-processing plant that is the main employer in a small town can fill its posts at a low wage, because workers have few other employers to turn to. So the wage tends to sit higher where workers are organised or scarce, and lower where the employer dominates the local market for labour.

blocks.heading: Government policy and the minimum wage
blocks.text: Government policy also shapes wages. The most direct tool is a minimum wage: the lowest wage, usually stated per hour, that an employer may legally pay a worker. South Africa has had a national minimum wage since 2019 and the United Kingdom since 1999, and Namibia also sets minimum wages by law. A minimum wage changes pay only if it is set above the market wage. Then low-paid workers who keep their jobs earn more, which may lift their living standards and their spending. The risk is to employment: at the higher wage employers seek fewer workers while more people want work, so an excess supply of labour opens up and unemployment among the low-paid may rise. How many jobs go depends on the elasticity of demand for that labour. Where it is elastic - because machines can replace the workers, or because wages are a large part of the firm's costs - the number of jobs falls noticeably; where it is inelastic, few jobs are lost. Set below the market wage, a minimum wage changes nothing, because employers already pay more. Government also sets wages directly as an employer, through the pay scales for teachers, nurses and police officers, and through laws requiring equal pay for work of equal value.

blocks.heading: A minimum wage on a farm
blocks.text: Suppose the market wage for general farm workers in a farming district is N$14 an hour, and the government sets a minimum wage of N$18 an hour - set above the market wage, so it binds. A farmer employing 20 workers for 200 hours a month each had a monthly wage bill of 20 x 200 x N$14 = N$56 000; at the minimum wage the same team costs 20 x 200 x N$18 = N$72 000, which is N$72 000 - N$56 000 = N$16 000 more. If the farm can switch to machines for harvesting, demand for that labour is elastic, and the farmer may cut the team to 15: five workers lose their jobs while the 15 who stay earn N$4 more an hour. If no machine can do the work, the farmer is likely to keep most of the team and meet the extra cost from lower profit or higher prices. The same policy helps one group of workers and may harm another, and which effect is larger depends on how easily the labour can be replaced.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The demand for workers comes from the product demand examined in topic 2.3 and from the firms of topic 3.5; the supply of workers depends on the occupational choices of this topic and on training decisions; and the government's role in funding training belongs to topic 4.1.
